description: The heel drop is the most famous tendon exercise in the world, used in clinics for decades, and it doubles as a brutal honest test. Today you lower off a step on one leg, grade the strongest tendon in your body, and learn how slow eccentrics rebuild it.

beats.text: UP ON TWO, DOWN ON ONE

scenes.narration: Stand on the edge of a step with your heels hanging off, holding a wall or rail for balance. Rise up onto your toes using both legs. Now lift one foot completely off the step, and lower the other heel down below the level of the step, slowly, counting three full seconds on the way down. That is one rep. Use both legs to get back up, and repeat on the same side. Count how many clean, slow, single-leg heel drops you can do before the tempo breaks or the calf gives up. Then switch sides. Two numbers, smaller one is the truth. Write it down. At the end of this video I will tell you why clinics around the world have used this exact movement for forty years.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN ORDINARY AND CLINIC-GRADE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twelve slow single-leg heel drops is where an ordinary Achilles becomes a clinic-grade one. Under six, the strongest tendon in your body is undertrained, which surprises everyone until they try this at an honest tempo. Over twenty, you own the kind of tendon that rehab specialists are trying to build in their patients, except yours came with a spring attached. The three-second rule is the whole exam. Almost anyone can drop fast. Lowering under total control, through the full range, with the heel sinking below the step, cannot be faked by strength, size or confidence.
scenes.sub: under 6: strongest tendon untrained - over 20: clinic-grade

lines: It stores energy like a spring
and returns it into every step.
beats.title: A SPRING, NOT A ROPE

beats.text: BUILT FOR LOADS YOU CANNOT LIFT

scenes.narration: Meet the strongest tendon in your body. The Achilles connects your calf to your heel, and in a single running step it handles loads of many times your bodyweight, forces no gym exercise comes close to matching. But calling it a rope undersells it. The Achilles is a spring. When your foot lands, it stretches and stores elastic energy. When you push off, it returns that energy into the step, which is why running feels bouncy instead of plodding when the system is healthy. The heel drop test loads this spring in its lengthening phase, called the eccentric phase, where the muscle works while the tendon stretches under control. That phase is where the spring is both strongest and most vulnerable, and it is the phase almost nobody trains on purpose. A man can have a big calf and a slow, sloppy heel drop, because the calf was only ever trained to shorten. The test asks the harder question: can the system brake? Braking is where tendons live, and braking is what this number grades. There is one more detail that makes this tendon special. It twists. The fibers of the Achilles spiral as they descend, like a rope wound for strength, and that spiral lets different parts of the calf load the spring at slightly different moments. It is engineering you would admire in a bridge cable, installed behind your ankle before you were born, waiting to be trained.

lines: Slow heel drops, twice a day,
beats.title: THE ALFREDSON IDEA

scenes.narration: This movement has a famous history. In the late nineteen nineties, a Swedish doctor named Alfredson, himself suffering from Achilles pain, built a program of slow, heavy heel drops, performed daily, and published results that changed tendon rehab forever. Patient after patient returned to sport on a program that looked too simple to work. The lesson reshaped how clinics think: a painful tendon usually does not need more rest. It needs the right load, dosed carefully, progressed patiently. Rest makes a tendon quieter and weaker. Loading makes it stronger and, over time, quieter too. Understand what that means for you. Your test today is not separate from the treatment. The heel drop is both. Performed slowly, at the edge of your ability, it grades the spring and rebuilds it in the same motion. Few exercises in the world can say that. It is also why this test has survived forty years of fitness fashions. Fashions change. Springs do not.

lines: Stiff for ten minutes is normal.
Worse every week is a message.
beats.title: READING THE TENDON

scenes.narration: Because this tendon talks, learn its language. The Achilles reports yesterday's dose the next morning, in stiffness. A few minutes of stiffness on your first steps is normal, even for healthy tendons. The signal that matters is the trend. If morning stiffness is shrinking week by week while your reps climb, the dose is right. If it is growing, the dose is too big, no matter how heroic the sessions felt. This is the monitoring system professionals use, and it costs you ten seconds of attention each morning. One more line, and it matters: tendons can be genuinely injured, and no video can see your tendon. If Achilles pain persists for weeks, sharpens, or comes with a lump that keeps growing, see a professional and get it examined in person. Train hard inside the rules, and respect the one signal that always outranks this channel: pain that keeps getting worse is information, not a challenge.

beats.text: SPRINTING IS HEEL DROPS AT SPEED

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage in the spring. Every landing you take loads the Achilles with a multiple of your bodyweight, so a lighter body is quite literally a cheaper spring to run. Heavy athletes are magnificent and their tendons pay magnificent prices, which is why big sprinters manage their Achilles like a fragile asset. You can train yours with more volume, more often, at lower risk, because each rep costs the tissue less. The braking practice that builds an elite spring is simply more affordable for you. Most men never train this at all. You can train it on a staircase, for free, at a discount they will never get.

Now we rebuild the spring together. Up on two legs, down on one, three seconds every lowering. Forty-five seconds of work, fifteen to rest, three rounds, weak side first. If the tempo breaks, the set is over. Brake like you mean it. Go.

lines: Let the mornings grade the dose.
beats.title: THE SPRING RULES

scenes.narration: Here is your week. Heel drops most days, in the rounds you just did, because this tendon responds to daily signals better than weekly punishment. But daily does not mean maximal. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: dropping fast when you tire. The fast drop is the exact rep that teaches nothing and risks everything. End the set when the tempo dies. Mistake two: skipping the below-step range. The heel must sink past the step level, because the deep part of the range is where the spring works hardest. Mistake three: ignoring the morning report. Stiffness trending up means smaller sessions, not more courage. One extra clean rep a week, judged by your mornings, is the pace that has rebuilt more Achilles tendons than any machine ever sold.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME STEP, SAME TEMPO
scenes.narration: So, your number, grading the weaker side as always. Under six: the strongest tendon you own is untrained, and now it has the most proven program in tendon history. Six to twelve: the spring is loading honestly, mornings will confirm it. Over twelve: a braking system most athletes would envy. Over twenty: clinic-grade, the number rehab patients spend months chasing. Put the smaller number in the comments. Just the reps. In thirty days we return to this step and lower again, slowly.
scenes.sub: comment your smaller number - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now the step will be the same, the tempo will be the same, and your spring will be a different spring. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave the smaller number in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Heel Drop Test Reveals Your Hidden Strength
